This was done in order to allow for direct comparisons between species.

### Free parameters

The free parameters of our models are the synaptic efficacies. The efficacies of synapses connecting each class of neurons are assumed to be identical, e.g., all P-EN to E-PG synapses have the same strength. Therefore, we have one free parameter for each synaptic class. Furthermore, we reduced the computational complexity of optimising the synaptic strengths by making the synaptic strength between some classes of neurons identical. The synaptic strengths of E-PG to P-EN and P-EG are identical as are the synaptic strengths of Delta7 to P-EN and P-EG. This is the minimum set of synaptic strengths that results in working ring attractors. We assumed that all synapses are excitatory apart from the synapses with Delta7 neurons on the presynaptic side, which were assumed to be inhibitory, as Kakaria and de Bivort, 2017 proposed. The synaptic strength was modelled as the number of $I_{P⁢S⁢C}$ unit equivalents flowing to the postsynaptic neuron per action potential.

Although our models are constrained by anatomical evidence, existing biological studies do not specify synaptic weights or connectivity. Based on the goal that each of the circuits should yield a functional ring attractor, an optimisation algorithm was used to search for synaptic strength combinations that resulted in working ring attractors. Both simulated annealing and particle swarm optimisation algorithms were used (Matlab Optimization Toolbox ‘simulannealbnd’ and ‘particleswarm’ functions); the first one converges quicker while the second one covers the search space more thoroughly. We constrained the acceptable solutions to those that produced an activity ‘bump’ with full width at half maximum (FWHM) of approximately 90° since this is the width that has been observed in fruit flies (Kim et al., 2017).

The objective function used to optimise the synaptic strengths $w_{i}$ was:

$$
argminw4(ϵ_{H1}(w)+ϵ_{H2}(w))+ϵ_{W1}(w)+ϵ_{W2}(w)+Np_{0}(w)s.tϵ_{H1}(w)=\frac{|H_{d}(t_{1})−H_{a}(w,t_{1})|}{360^{∘}}ϵ_{H2}(w)=\frac{|H_{d}(t_{2})−H_{a}(w,t_{2})|}{360^{∘}}ϵ_{W1}(w)=\frac{|90^{∘}−W_{a}(w,t_{1})|}{360^{∘}}ϵ_{W2}(w)=\frac{|90^{∘}−W_{a}(w,t_{2})|}{360^{∘}}p_{0}(w)=\frac{1}{N}\sumi=1N(e^{−|w_{i}|})^{2}0\leqw_{1}\leq1000\leqw_{2}\leq1000\leqw_{3}\leq100−100\leqw_{4}\leq0−100\leqw_{5}\leq0
$$

where $ϵ_{H⁢1}$, $ϵ_{H⁢2}$, $ϵ_{W⁢1}$ and $ϵ_{W⁢2}$ are the error factors measured as deviations from the desired values. $p_{0}$ is used to penalise synaptic strengths being too close to 0. N is the number of synaptic strengths $w_{i}$. $H_{d}(t)$ is the desired activity ‘bump’ heading at time t, while $H_{a}⁢(𝐰,t)$ is the actual measured activity ‘bump’ heading at time t given a model with synaptic strengths $w$. $W_{a}(w,t)$ is the actual measured width of the activity ‘bump’ at time t (measured as the full width at half maximum). The constraints in Equation 7 specify that the synapses with Delta7 neurons at their presynaptic side are inhibitory (negative) and all others are excitatory (positive). Synaptic weights were initialised with values −0.01 or 0.01 depending on whether the negative only or positive only constraint was applied. During optimisation the spiking models were used to run the simulations and search the space of synaptic strengths. The synaptic strength sets that resulted from multiple runs were manually tested to verify the results. The objective function was used to optimise the synaptic strengths separately for each of the models: the fruit fly, the locust, and the hybrid-species model.

### Sensitivity analysis and parameter noise

For the sensitivity analysis, white Gaussian noise was added to the membrane parameters of neurons (conductance and capacitance) as well as to the synaptic efficacies, using the formula

$$
v_{i}=v_{nominal}+\frac{x}{100}v_{nominal}ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩(\mu,\sigma^{2})
$$

where $v_{i}$ is the resulting noisy value of the parameter with $i={1,2,…,M}$ and $M$ being the number of parameters. $v_{n⁢o⁢m⁢i⁢n⁢a⁢l}$ is the nominal value of the parameter, $x\in[0,100]$ is the percentage of noise to be added to the nominal value, ε is a random variable sampled from the Gaussian distribution with $\mu=0$ and $\sigma^{2}=1$. When noise was added to the conductance and capacitance of neurons the resulting values were clipped to a minimum of 0 because conductance and capacitance values cannot be negative. For measuring the tolerance to inter-hemispheric synaptic asymmetry we altered the P-EN to E-PG synapses in one hemisphere by different amounts in the range −100% to 100%.

The number of successful trials was counted in each condition. The criterion for a successful trial was that the activity ‘bump’ transitioned from an initial stimulus-driven heading to a second stimulus-driven heading with an error of less that ±45° and subsequently the second heading was maintained for at least 3 s. The criterion used for judging jump versus gradual transition of the heading signal was that for the transition to be considered a jump the intervening neurons between the origin and end location must not become maximally active during the transition.

Summary:

This study uses existing quantitative neuroanatomy data in Drosophila and locust to construct a connectivity matrix of the presumptive ring attractor circuit used in navigation. Using a simplification of the connectivity the authors show a “hidden” ring attractor in the locust that has a distinct connectivity profile from Drosophila. Using simulations the authors examine the consequences of the different connectivity in each species and conclude that the locust has a more robust internal representation of heading, with possible ethological consequences.

Essential revisions:

1) Reviewers were concerned about a lack of detail and possible ambiguity in how the reduced/effective connectivity diagrams are obtained. The authors should revise the diagrams and accompanying text, providing additional explanatory figures if necessary.

2) Conclusions are based on the contribution of connectivity to dynamics alone, yet the choice of modelling detail is inconsistent. The authors should show that the most parsimonious assumptions (e.g. rate-based models) corroborate the results and include robustness analysis of the more “detailed” simulations. Statements about the biological realism should be appropriately edited.

Reviewer #1:

Summary:

This work uses existing quantitative neuroanatomy data in Drosophila and locust to construct a connectivity matrix of the presumptive ring attractor circuit used in navigation. They show using an elegant topological analysis that there is a “hidden” ring attractor in the locust that has a distinct connectivity profile. Using integrate and fire based simulations the authors examine the consequences of the different connectivity in each species and conclude that the locust has a more robust internal representation of heading, with possible ethological consequences. The manuscript is beautifully presented and highly relevant, however there are unfortunate and gravely misleading statements about the assumptions in the model that need to be addressed. A final, positive attribute of the work is an important broad message that cautions against drawing overly general conclusions from the details of a heavily studied model system, something the community urgently needs to be reminded of. If the substantive concerns can be addressed the manuscript could make a valuable contribution to systems/circuit neuroscience.

Major comments:

1) The conclusions of this study rest on the assumption that all of the neuronal properties in both circuits are identical and conform to simple integrate and fire dynamics with a linear membrane. This is almost certainly false but little to no mention is made of the “potential consequences” of this assumption. No attempt has been made to test the sensitivity of the conclusions to this assumption, even though this is possible without resorting to “multicompartmental models”. The only acknowledgement of this is made in the Discussion which simply asserts that this is essentially a technical simulation detail that would not add “tangible gains”. Worse still, the authors claim elsewhere that the model “uses realistic biophysical properties”. The point extends beyond heterogeneity and it is a little painful to have to remind the authors of how false their statement is; the writing indicates they are almost certainly aware of this. Intrinsic properties alone can provide short term memory that would radically alter the responsiveness of a circuit and there are thousands of neurophysiological studies that make this very clear. The manuscript could have been written in a more scientifically honest and circumspect way, pointing out these issues without necessarily exhaustively addressing all of them. Instead, unfortunately, the authors have chosen to mislead their readers. This makes the manuscript unpublishable in its present form.

2) The optimization algorithm and the results obtained from it are inadequately described and validated. There are many ways of using particle swarm optimisation, for example, and there are initial values/distributions/search limits that affect the results. None of this is described. Making code available is not a substitute.

3) The choice of detail in the modelling is a little bizarre. On one hand, it is clear that this is an abstract model, placing synaptic connectivity above all else. This would suggest a rate based model. Instead, integrate and fire models are used that have additional parameters as well as a highly detailed spike waveform inserted in place of a spike event. This is a cosmetic feature that only obscures the results. Do any of the conclusions depend on these decisions, and if not, why were these decisions made? Again, this decision unfortunately looks like an attempt to convince the reader of biophysical realism in a trivial and inconsequential way, while ducking the substantive issues.

4) I suggest the authors build up their modelling approach from a truly minimal (e.g. rate based) case, proceeding to details like spiking and proper heterogeneity. This would allow readers to get some sense of which details “may” actually matter. The manuscript should also be more scientifically honest about the limitations of the study because these are necessary given available data and tractability. The manuscript would actually be stronger if this were made clear.

Reviewer #3:

In this manuscript, Pisokas et al. consider a neural circuit that is conserved across insect species: the reciprocal connections between the protocerebral bridge and ellipsoid body. There is evidence this circuit supports goal-directed navigation in several species. Using neuroanatomical data from locust and fruit flies, the authors simulate the dynamics of this circuit in each species. There are three major conclusions. First, the connectivity of the locust circuit has the potential to implement a ring-attractor. Second, the simulated dynamics in the locust model reiterate the qualitative physiological results consistent with a ring-attractor. Third, in a comparative analysis, the authors determine that differences between the locust and fly circuits (different presynaptic extents in inhibitory PB neurons and reciprocal connections between P-ENs and E-PGs in the locust) render the locust spatial dynamics more stable, but also slower to respond to stimulus changes. The authors speculate that these differences may relate to differences in the ethology of the species. The comparative circuit dynamics approach is innovative and interesting, and this may be an early example of a technique that becomes increasingly valuable and prevalent as more connectomic data is produced in non-model species.

The authors do a persuasive job of justifying these conclusions. The conclusions are relatively mild in their ambitions, and there are ways to restructure this approach that might offer more in terms of substantive conclusions and less of a feeling of a rather ad hoc, piecewise analysis. For example, the authors could delineate ~6 circuits: fly, locust, hybrid, locust without PEGs, fly without PEGs, hybrid without PEGs, as the rows of a matrix, in which the columns are analyses, bump movement speed, rate of change, number of locations, stability etc. If that's too much for a table, then the core figures could have the same panel arrangement of the same ~6 (or how many ever) circuit configurations. This is just an idea, and might be outside the scope of revisions because the authors have achieved their stated goal of those three main conclusions.

As for presentation, the figures are generally clear. The text is a bit wordy, but it makes it more palateable to get through all the neuroanatomical jargon. There are a fair number of typos/grammatical issues as indicated below. We almost certainly did not catch them all, so the authors will have to do careful editing. Because the writing is not super dense, the typos did not really interfere with understanding.

Note: This review was done by a π and grad student in the same lab, so it's long because it’s the consensus of both reviews. We did not find any major concerns that would call into question the major conclusions.

More substantive concerns:

– Clearer definitions of ring attractor would be helpful early on. What are the requirements in neuroanatomy for a circuit to have the structure of a ring-attractor. What are the requirements in physiological dynamics and stimulus response for the behavior of a circuit to be consistent with a ring attractor? Operational definitions would be particularly valuable because the authors frame their investigation as a test of the existence of such properties in the circuitry.

– More needs to be said in the Results section about the synapse strength parameterization. What was the cost function for this optimization, etc. Even in the Materials and methods section, this is covered rather briefly.

– The hybrid model is good, but the authors might consider titrating the number of glomeruli with postsynaptic sites in the Delta7 neurons from 3 to 7, and show the response in stimulus shift + other "ring attractor" behaviors. This is not necessary to the conclusions they present, but would be interesting from a theoretical perspective and there may be other species with morphologies like that.

– Unclear why 9th glomerulus in fly is okay to exclude from Figure 3.

– We wondered if the wraparound of the 8th tile to the 1st tile in locust is justified. If E-PG5 innervates tiles T5 and T6 and glomeruli G5 of the PB, would E-PG8 innervate the right-most wedges of Figure 4, i.e. T8 and T1? Then, as P-EN5 innervates tiles T5 and T6, does P-EN8 innervate T8 and both half-tiles of T1 on opposite sides of the crescent?

– Please make clear how the effective circuits are different from the full connectivity matrices, is the former simplified to give intuition? Are there reasons for reducing the real connectivity matrix to the effective matrix other than computational simplicity?

– Why was the test of the role of P-EGs done by an interhemispheric mismatch? (Also, what does this mean, since the CX is on the midline.) Simply removing that population from the simulation would seem more in line with how other hypotheses were tested.

– The discussion on the closed ring shape of the Dipteran EB confused me. The physical shape doesn't matter much (other than in timing details) if the network connectivity is the same? Why would the closure of the physical ring matter for P-EN to E-PG connectivity, except at the suture, and if it's only there that it might matter, the text needs to say this.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that heading direction circuits in insect central complex (CX) resemble ring attractors, based on prior experimental work in fruit flies and locusts. These circuits show conserved topographic structure across species but with anatomical differences at the single-neuron level.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C27 and C39 collectively establish the background context from prior literature about heading direction circuits in insects. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations to experimental and theoretical work (C8-C23, C38), anatomical descriptions (C13-C15), and comparative observations (C39). The claims appropriately distinguish between established knowledge and the current study's contributions.

results.result: Three main anatomical differences exist between fruit fly and locust CX circuits: (1) the locust EB is crescent-shaped rather than ring-shaped, (2) locusts have 8 PB glomeruli per hemisphere versus 9 in fruit flies, and (3) Delta7 neurons show different dendritic distribution patterns—uniform in fruit flies but restricted to specific glomeruli in locusts.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C51 describe anatomical differences supported by both citations to prior anatomical studies (C46, C47, C49, C50) and visual evidence in Figures 1-2. The observations are consistent with established comparative neuroanatomy and provide the foundation for the modeling work. The anatomical characterizations are well-documented in the literature cited.

results.result: The inhibitory connectivity patterns differ fundamentally between species: in fruit flies, each Delta7 neuron inhibits all other Delta7 neurons (global inhibition), while in locusts, each Delta7 neuron inhibits only a subset with weakening strengths toward neighbors (local inhibition).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 and C67 describe the derived inhibitory connectivity patterns shown in Figure 2 and supported by anatomical citations (C53). The global versus local inhibition distinction is consistent with the anatomical observations and aligns with prior experimental findings (C54 cites Kim et al., 2017). The inference from anatomy to functional connectivity is reasonable given the overlap-based synapse assumptions.

results.result: Despite anatomical differences, the effective circuit structure is equivalent between species, forming closed ring attractors organized in eight octants with identical functional roles for each neuron class. Different anatomical solutions achieve ring closure: the torus-shaped EB in fruit flies versus cross-innervation of medial glomeruli in locusts.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58, C61, C64, C118-C121 describe the core finding of circuit equivalence shown in Figures 3-5. The derivation of effective circuits from anatomical data is methodologically sound, using graph-theoretic analysis to reveal functional equivalence despite structural differences. The identification of convergent evolutionary solutions (C118-C119) is well-supported by the circuit analysis. This represents a major conceptual advance.

results.result: The locust circuit contains reciprocal P-EN to E-PG connections within the same octant that are absent in fruit flies, resulting from a half-tile versus whole-tile shift in P-EN synaptic domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 identify a key structural difference shown in Figures 3-4. The observation is clearly documented in the figures and follows logically from the anatomical projection patterns. This difference has functional consequences explored in later results regarding noise tolerance.

results.result: Optimization of synaptic strengths revealed consistent patterns: P-EN to E-PG and P-EG to E-PG synapses were weakest, E-PG to P-EG/P-EN synapses were strongest, and inhibitory Delta7 synapses were stronger in locusts than fruit flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 report results from the optimization procedure shown in Figure 6. The optimization methodology is described in Materials and Methods, using biologically plausible constraints. The predicted synaptic strength patterns are internally consistent and provide testable predictions. However, these are model predictions rather than experimental measurements, which should be noted.

results.result: Both circuits operate as ring attractors but with distinct activity patterns: locust Delta7 neurons show strong heading-dependent modulation with silent neurons at the bump location, while fruit fly Delta7 neurons show minimal modulation (~10%). Locust neurons are consistently tuned ~20% more narrowly than fruit fly neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C82 describe simulation results shown in Figure 7 and Tables 1-2. The differences in Delta7 firing patterns (C73-C76) are clearly demonstrated and consistent with the global versus local inhibition architecture. The prediction of pronounced firing rate variation in locusts (C73-C74) is supported by existing electrophysiological data (C77). The tuning width differences (C78-C82) are quantified in the tables.

results.result: The fruit fly heading signal can jump abruptly between states while the locust circuit exhibits gradual transitions. This difference is due to connectivity rather than neuron model choice, as confirmed by both spiking and rate-based implementations.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 describe a key dynamical difference shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The validation using both spiking and rate-based models (C84-C85) strengthens the conclusion that connectivity drives the difference. This is a well-supported finding with clear mechanistic basis.

results.result: Hybrid-species modeling demonstrates that the inhibition pattern is the main determinant of response dynamics: changing from global to local inhibition produces gradual transitions. The fruit fly circuit stabilizes to new headings in approximately half the time of the locust circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 describe results from the hybrid-species model shown in Figure 8. The experimental design effectively isolates the effect of inhibition pattern by swapping only the Delta7 connectivity. The quantification of response times (C87, C90) provides clear evidence for the functional consequences of the anatomical differences. This is a well-controlled computational experiment.

results.result: Systematic variation of inhibitory synaptic domain width (σ) reveals that transition mode depends on both σ and angular heading change magnitude. Low σ values produce gradual transitions while high σ produces abrupt jumps, with σ=0.8 approximating the locust pattern based on dendritic density estimates.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 describe parameter exploration shown in Figure 9. The systematic variation of σ provides insight into the relationship between anatomy and dynamics. However, the choice of σ=0.8 for the locust (C94) is based on visual estimates of dendritic density rather than quantitative measurements, introducing some uncertainty. The general conclusion about inhibition pattern importance (C95) is well-supported.

results.result: Both circuits have discrete attractor states, but locust attractor states are more stable and clearly delineated than fruit fly states, which show wider distributions of bump locations, indicating greater robustness to drift and noise in the locust.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 describe attractor basin analysis shown in Figure 10. The experimental design (applying stimuli at varying positions and measuring final bump location) appropriately tests attractor stability. The quantification of standard deviations provides clear evidence for the stability difference. The conclusion about noise robustness (C99) follows logically from the data.

results.result: The locust circuit is significantly more tolerant to structural (synaptic) noise than the fruit fly circuit. Comparison with the hybrid-species model demonstrates that reciprocal P-EN to E-PG connections provide this increased robustness.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 describe noise tolerance experiments shown in Figure 11A. The comparison between locust and hybrid-species models effectively isolates the contribution of P-EN to E-PG reciprocal connections. The inference (C101) is well-supported by the data showing the hybrid-species model has intermediate robustness between fruit fly and locust.

results.result: P-EG neurons substantially increase robustness to synaptic strength imbalances in P-EN to E-PG synapses in both species, as demonstrated by comparing models with and without P-EG neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 describe ablation experiments shown in Figure 11B-C. The experimental design (removing P-EG neurons and testing asymmetry tolerance) appropriately tests the functional role of these neurons. The results clearly show increased tolerance range with P-EG neurons present. The conclusion about P-EG contribution to stability (C103) is well-supported.

results.result: The locust model is more robust to neuronal heterogeneity in membrane properties than the fruit fly model, but the distinct transition regimes (gradual versus jump) are preserved regardless of heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 describe heterogeneity experiments shown in Figure 12 and Figure 12—figure supplement 1. The systematic variation of membrane parameters tests model robustness to biological variability. The preservation of transition dynamics (C105) despite heterogeneity strengthens the conclusion that connectivity determines these dynamics. The results are clearly presented.

results.result: Both models reproduce experimental response dynamics to P-EN stimulation. The heading signal shift rate increases exponentially with stimulation strength, more steeply in fruit flies, which also require lower stimulus thresholds for initiating bump shifting.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 describe validation against experimental data (Turner-Evans et al., 2017) shown in Figures 13-14. The reproduction of experimental dynamics (C106) validates the models. The quantification of exponential relationships (C107-C109) and interpretation regarding saccade tracking (C110) are well-supported by the data. This provides important experimental validation.

results.result: Continuous angular velocity input causes the heading signal to wrap around from one edge of the PB to the other in both models, independent of EB physical shape, supported by the effective closed ring structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 describe wrap-around behavior from simulations. The observation (C111) is clearly demonstrated, and the conclusion that this is independent of EB shape (C112) follows from observing it in both species. The connection to the effective ring structure (C113) is logical. This demonstrates functional equivalence despite anatomical differences.

results.result: The study demonstrates that the locust circuit can operate as a ring attractor, with differences in inhibition pattern enabling faster fruit fly responses to heading changes while additional recurrent connections render the locust circuit more noise-tolerant. These differences may reflect behavioral adaptations: fast saccades in fruit flies versus sustained heading maintenance in migratory locusts.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7, C114-C116, C122-C123 synthesize the main findings and their behavioral interpretation. The core results (C4-C6) are well-supported by the modeling and analysis. The behavioral interpretations (C114-C115) are supported by citations to behavioral studies. The evolutionary speculation (C116) is appropriately tentative. The mechanistic conclusions (C122-C123) accurately summarize the findings. This represents the paper's main contribution.

results.result: The preservation of the heading tracking circuit across 400 million years of evolutionary divergence suggests it is an essential, potentially fundamental, part of the insect brain.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 makes an evolutionary inference based on the demonstrated circuit conservation. The inference is reasonable given the functional equivalence despite anatomical differences, though it is necessarily speculative about evolutionary history. The claim is appropriately qualified as a suggestion rather than a definitive conclusion.
